title: Academic Reading — Demo Test 1
description: Original practice test. Three passages, 40 questions, 60 minutes.

passages.title: The Bees of the City
passages.body:
**A**  For most of the twentieth century, the city was regarded as a hostile place for wildlife. Yet in the last decade, rooftop hives have appeared on offices, hotels and apartment blocks in London, Paris, New York and Tokyo. Urban beekeeping has become a hobby, a corporate gift and, for some, a symbol of environmental responsibility.

**B**  There are practical reasons why bees can do well in cities. Gardens, parks and railway embankments provide a remarkable variety of flowers, often in bloom for longer than farmland crops. Cities are also warmer than the surrounding countryside: the "urban heat island" effect can extend the flowering season by several weeks. And, crucially, urban gardens generally contain far fewer pesticides than the fields of intensive agriculture.

**C**  Not everyone is convinced that more hives are good news. Critics point out that the number of managed hives in some cities has risen faster than the available forage. When thousands of colonies compete for the same flowers, even strong colonies can struggle, and the result may be weaker bees rather than healthier ones. "Beekeeping is an agricultural activity, not a conservation measure," one ecologist argues.

**D**  Research supports a cautious view. A 2019 study of London's honeybees found that, in areas with a high density of hives, wild bee species were less diverse, possibly because managed colonies take a large share of the pollen and nectar. The study did not show that beekeeping causes the decline, but it did suggest that adding hives is not a reliable way to help wild pollinators.

**E**  So what does help? Ecologists tend to agree on a short list: plant more flowers, leave wild areas unmown, avoid pesticides, and provide nesting sites. These measures support the many wild bee species that do not live in hives at all — solitary bees, bumblebees and hoverflies. A single flowering hedge can do more for local biodiversity than a rooftop hive.

**F**  None of this means that hobby beekeeping is pointless. It can raise awareness of pollinators, and a well-managed hive produces honey without harming wild species if the local environment has enough flowers. But the claim that keeping bees "saves the bees" is misleading. The insects most in need of help are rarely the ones in a box.

passages.title: Why We Forget
passages.body:
**A**  Forgetting is often treated as a failure, something to be prevented with effort or technology. In fact, most everyday forgetting is a normal consequence of how memory works: the brain is constantly deciding what to keep and what to discard. Without this filtering, we would be overwhelmed by irrelevant detail.

**B**  The first systematic study of forgetting was carried out by Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885. Using himself as a subject, he memorised lists of nonsense syllables and tested his recall at intervals. The resulting "forgetting curve" showed that memory loss is steepest in the first hours and days after learning, then gradually levels off. More than a century later, the shape of the curve has proved remarkably robust.

**C**  One explanation is interference. New memories can disrupt older ones, and older memories can make it harder to form new ones. Sleep appears to play an important role here: during sleep, the brain replays and consolidates recent experience, which seems to protect memories from interference.

**D**  A different account emphasises retrieval failure. Memories may be stored but inaccessible without the right cue. The tip-of-the-tongue experience — knowing that you know a word but being unable to produce it — is a familiar example. Recall is also context-dependent: material learned in one room is often remembered better in the same room.

**E**  Some researchers now argue that forgetting is not merely a flaw but a feature. Clearing outdated information allows the mind to generalise and to respond flexibly to a changing world. On this view, the mind is less like a warehouse and more like a library that regularly removes books no longer borrowed. Forgetting, in other words, is part of remembering well.

passages.title: The Second-Hand Economy
passages.body:
**A**  Buying used goods was once associated with necessity, a choice made by people who could not afford anything better. In the past decade, resale has acquired a different image. Online marketplaces and resale apps have made it easy to buy and sell everything from designer coats to children's bicycles, and second-hand shopping is now presented as stylish, thrifty and responsible.

**B**  The most powerful driver, however, is money. As living costs have risen, households have looked for ways to reduce spending and to recover value from things they no longer use. A coat that can be resold is cheaper to own than one that cannot.

**C**  The environmental case is less straightforward than it appears. Reusing a product does avoid the emissions of making a new one, and extending a garment's life is clearly better than throwing it away. But the benefits depend on how the item is transported, how often it is actually worn, and what happens to it afterwards. Returns and long-distance shipping can reduce the savings considerably.

**D**  Brands have responded in different ways. Some have launched their own resale platforms, hoping to keep control of the second-hand market and to attract customers who would not pay full price. Others worry that resale could take sales from new products, and some have been accused of designing goods that are hard to repair.

**E**  Behind the friendly interface, resale has practical problems. Authentication is difficult and expensive: distinguishing genuine items from counterfeits requires trained staff and specialist equipment. Sorting centres also depend on large numbers of workers doing repetitive and sometimes precarious jobs.

**F**  What happens next will depend partly on regulation. Several governments are considering rules on product durability and on the "right to repair", which would make resale easier and more trustworthy. Standardised labels for second-hand condition are also being discussed. The market is likely to keep growing, but its environmental reputation will depend on whether these problems are addressed.
